CausalChain: Upregulated GEMIN5 -> Impaired assembly of DNA repair complexes (via altered mRNA stability/translation of repair factors) -> Reduced double-strand break repair via break-induced replication -> Genomic instability -> Enhanced metastasis and poor liver cancer prognosis; Additionally, dysregulated FUS -> Further impairment of repair enzyme activity and signaling
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, aberrant overexpression of GEMIN5 disrupts the precise assembly of DNA repair complexes by altering the stability and translation efficiency of mRNAs that encode essential repair proteins, particularly those involved in break-induced replication. Concurrently, the dysregulation (be it through mislocalization, post-translational modification, or altered expression levels) of FUS exacerbates this impairment by further dysregulating enzyme activities and signal transduction within the repair cascade. This dual-axis disruption leads to a marked reduction in the efficiency of the double-strand break repair mechanism, thereby promoting genomic instability, tumor invasion, metastasis, and ultimately poorer prognosis. This study will employ advanced technologies—including single-cell transcriptomics to monitor RNA-binding protein profiles, CRISPR screens to perturb and validate key regulatory nodes, and high-resolution protein-RNA interactome assays—to delineate the causal relationship and validate this novel mechanistic pathway.
Abstract: We propose that in liver cancer, the upregulation of GEMIN5, together with an altered interaction and dysregulation of RNA‐binding protein FUS, disrupts the post‐transcriptional regulation of key DNA repair factors, thereby impairing the assembly and function of DNA repair complexes. Specifically, overexpressed GEMIN5 destabilizes and misregulates the translation of mRNAs encoding critical repair proteins, principally affecting the break-induced replication (BIR) pathway—a normally error‐prone double-strand break repair process. In parallel, FUS dysregulation further interferes with repair enzyme activity and signaling, compounding the reduced repair capacity. This cascade of events culminates in significant genomic instability, which promotes tumor invasion, metastasis, and poorer outcomes in liver neoplasms. Leveraging contemporary technologies such as single-cell RNA sequencing, CRISPR-based gene perturbation, and high-resolution protein-RNA interaction mapping, our approach aims to validate the mechanistic causality of this pathway and identify novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that GEMIN5 upregulation and FUS dysregulation impair double-strand break repair through break-induced replication, leading to genomic instability and poor outcomes. Our revised hypothesis retains this core causal chain but refines and clarifies each step: (1) We specify that GEMIN5 promotes an impaired assembly of DNA repair complexes via its regulation of mRNA stability and translation of repair factors; (2) We further pinpoint that FUS’s dysregulation may occur through diverse mechanisms affecting its interaction with repair proteins, thereby amplifying repair deficiencies; (3) We explicitly justify the focus on break-induced replication by linking it to the observed error-prone repair and resultant genomic instability; and (4) We integrate modern technological capabilities—such as single-cell RNA sequencing, CRISPR perturbation assays, and advanced interactome mapping—to enhance the empirical testability and practical implementability of the hypothesis. These modifications address critical mechanistic gaps and align the hypothesis more closely with contemporary molecular biology research methods.
